Prevention: Plough to expose the soil-living thrips pupae to predators.
Avoid planting tomatoes after onions (a host of thrips).
Marigold ( Tagetes ) plants around field, but not into the field, because their yellow flowers can attract thrips away from tomatoes.
Irrigate regularly to reduce susceptibility of plants to thrips damage.
Note that wet conditions can promote certain diseases.
Monitoring: Thrips are very small and thin insect pests.
They are light grey to greenish, but difficult to see.
Thrips cause tiny scars on leaves and fruits.
Damaged leaves become papery and may curl and drop.
Thrips often attack during the flowering stage.
Search in the flowers and on fruits for thrips, and for tiny scars on leaves, flowers and fruits.
Scout particularly just prior and then during flowering stage.
When 5 to 10 plants per small <0.25 ha field have damage symptoms or many thrips in flowers and on fruits, then consider action.
Direct Control: Liquid soap spray (stir 3 table spoons liquid soap, e.g.

Cera- liquid, with 4 litres water) is only effective during moist conditions, and when sprayed at least 2 x in a week interval.Neem extract sprays max 3 times (2.5-3 litres/ha or 50-60 ml/20 litres water, or 25 to 50 g neem seed cake or powder /litre water).
Garlic bulb oil spray (20 fine shopped garlic cloves soaked 1 d in 100 ml mineral oil, then + 10 ml soap, stir, + 2 litre water, stir) over plants max 2 x, in min 1 week interval.
Restrictions: Avoid spraying, because heavy thrips infestation usually only occurs late in the cropping cycle.
Then tomatoes have flowers and pesticides kill bees.
Later on, chemicals can poison fruits ready for harvesting.
Only earlier in season in rare cases of heavy infestations you may consider sprays, reaching upper and lower surface of leaves.
When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label.
